name: 14-dns
description:
Names instead of addresses: **dns** answers for the zone `lab.test`, and forwards other names to a public DNS server.

| Container | Address on `192.168.60.0/24` (switch **lan**) | Name |
|---|---|---|
| dns | `192.168.60.53`, plus `nat0` (to forward queries) | `ns.lab.test` |
| www | `192.168.60.80` | `www.lab.test`, `web.lab.test` (an alias) |
| pc | `192.168.60.10` | uses dns as its DNS server |

## Try it
1. **Deploy**. In pc's **Console**:
   ```
   cat /etc/resolv.conf
   dig www.lab.test
   dig web.lab.test
   curl http://www.lab.test
   ```
2. A name that doesn't exist, and one from the internet:
   ```
   dig nothere.lab.test
   dig example.com
   curl -I https://example.com
   ```
   The name resolves, but the page doesn't load. Why?
3. Click the **pc–lan** cable and **Capture** while you run `dig www.lab.test`: one UDP packet to port 53, one back.
4. In dns's console, watch the queries arrive: `tail -f /var/log/dnsmasq.log`.
5. Add a name: in dns's startup commands, add `--host-record=mail.lab.test,192.168.60.25 \` under the `www` line, then **Stop** and **Start** dns and `dig mail.lab.test` from pc.

> [!NOTE]
> `ping www` works in any DockerLab lab without DNS, because DockerLab writes the containers' names into `/etc/hosts`. That's why this lab uses names under `lab.test`, which only the DNS server knows.

## Questions
- [ ] Look at `dig`'s output: which section holds the answer, and what's the TTL?
- [ ] Why does `dig example.com` work for pc, which has no internet access?
- [ ] What's the difference between `www.lab.test`'s A record and `web.lab.test`'s CNAME?

nodes.name: dns
nodes.startup:
# A DNS server for the zone lab.test (dnsmasq); other names are forwarded to 1.1.1.1
pkill -x dnsmasq 2>/dev/null
dnsmasq --interface=eth0 --bind-interfaces --no-hosts --no-resolv --server=1.1.1.1 \
  --local=/lab.test/ \
  --host-record=ns.lab.test,192.168.60.53 \
  --host-record=www.lab.test,192.168.60.80 \
  --cname=web.lab.test,www.lab.test \
  --log-queries --log-facility=/var/log/dnsmasq.log

nodes.name: www
nodes.startup:
# The web page cat > /var/www/index.html < $(hostname)

Hello from $(hostname)

You reached www.lab.test by name, through the lab's DNS server.

HTML # The web server: BusyBox httpd on port 80, serving /var/www pkill -x httpd 2>/dev/null; busybox-extras httpd -p 80 -h /var/www

nodes.name: pc
nodes.startup:
# Use the lab's DNS server, and try names in lab.test first
printf 'nameserver 192.168.60.53\nsearch lab.test\n' > /etc/resolv.conf

images.dockerlab/host:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# Everyday tools for an end host: full ip, packet capture, DNS lookups, web requests
RUN apk add --no-cache iproute2 tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils
images.dockerlab/web:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# A small web server (BusyBox httpd), plus the end-host tools: full ip, packet capture, DNS lookups, web requests
RUN apk add --no-cache busybox-extras iproute2 tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils
RUN mkdir -p /var/www
images.dockerlab/gateway:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# A home-router style gateway: NAT (iptables) plus DHCP and DNS (dnsmasq), and the usual network tools
RUN apk add --no-cache dnsmasq iproute2 iptables tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils

# nat-on: masquerade traffic leaving through the NAT interface (nat0).
# Safe to run more than once; use it in startup commands.
RUN printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' \
      'iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -o nat0 -j MASQUERADE 2>/dev/null || iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o nat0 -j MASQUERADE' \
      > /usr/local/bin/nat-on && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nat-on
